entry.title: Bridging the Gap Between Warehouse Execution and Serialization
entry.content:
SAP EWM · SAP ATTP · Pharma Supply Chain

Bridging the Gap Between Warehouse Execution and Serialization

A practitioner's deep dive into the SAP EWM–ATTP integration add-on — what it is, how it works, and what it changes for pharmaceutical supply chains.

 
Harshendu Dave & Gaurav Kochhar · SAP Solution Architects
 

1. Introduction to the EWM–ATTP Add-on

In today's regulated global supply chain, serialization is a core operational mandate. Without standard integration, warehouses face the "swivel-chair" dilemma — scanning items once for physical inventory and again for logical serialization, or relying on fragile custom middleware.

1.1 Why the EWM–ATTP Add-on

The SAP EWM add-on for ATTP solves the serialization bottleneck by turning compliance into a background process. Here is the business value it delivers:

Eliminating the double-scan tax. Every extra second an operator spends switching systems multiplies across thousands of daily transactions. The add-on enables a single point of data entry. When an operator scans a case to put it on a pallet via their RF gun, EWM registers the physical movement and ATTP instantly records the logical aggregation — one scan, both worlds updated.

The compliance safety net. Without real-time integration, a warehouse might physically ship a product flagged as "recalled," "stolen," or "expired" in ATTP. The add-on validates serial numbers synchronously during the RF scan and acts as an immediate stop-gate. If ATTP says a serial number is invalid, EWM blocks the operator from proceeding.

Zero-latency dispatch. In regulated industries you cannot legally dispatch until the exact serial numbers and their hierarchies are accurately reported. With the add-on, the moment the final goods issue is posted in EWM, ATTP already has the perfectly nested hierarchy ready to trigger outbound compliance messages.

Eradicating spaghetti architecture. Without the add-on, integrating a high-volume warehouse with a serialization database requires heavy custom development — interfaces and middleware that become a liability during upgrades. The add-on provides a clean, SAP-supported architecture that evolves as regulations change, drastically lowering total cost of ownership.

1.2 What Is the EWM–ATTP Add-on

The EWM add-on for ATTP is a standardized integration layer that synchronizes physical warehouse movements with the track-and-trace repository. It embeds serialization checks directly into standard EWM Radio Frequency (RF) processes.

Warehouse operators use their familiar handheld scanners and perform standard warehouse activities — picking, packing, receiving — while the system automatically verifies serial numbers in ATTP in real time and posts the relevant events in the background.

 

Key design principle: EWM remains the process driver. ATTP remains the serialization authority. The add-on ensures they stay synchronized at every step — automatically, in real time — without requiring warehouse operators to work in two systems.

1.3 Prerequisites

A. Business readiness — A defined process strategy to map which physical processes require serialization data capture, and which regulatory markets are in scope.

B. System connectivity — An operational SAP EWM (embedded or decentralised) and an active SAP ATTP instance, with RFC destinations and logical systems established. See Section 2 for full detail.

C. Master data alignment — Products, business partners, and locations must be synchronized across ERP, EWM, and ATTP:

  • In S/4HANA embedded EWM, master data is extended automatically — both live in the same system.
  • In decentralised EWM, customers/vendors (Business Partners), plants, and materials must be explicitly distributed from ERP to EWM via IDocs/ALE in S/4HANA landscapes, or CIF in older ECC+SCM landscapes.
  • The same master data (GTINs, business partners, plant references) must also be aligned from ERP to ATTP via SAP standard integration reports.

D. Transactional data — Deliveries are integrated from ERP to ATTP using SAP standard integration reports. With the right configuration this is automatic. Deliveries are distributed from ERP to EWM via qRFC.

1.4 System Architecture

Two primary deployment models exist. The choice between them shapes every aspect of the integration design.

 
S/4HANA with embedded EWM - EWM runs inside S/4HANA. ERP and EWM share the same database. ATTP is a separate system connected via RFC. Simplest architecture — one fewer system boundary.
 
Decentralised EWM - EWM runs as a standalone system separate from ERP. Three-system landscape: ERP, EWM, and ATTP each with their own installation. Common in brownfield pharma accounts.
 
  
Fig 1 — System architecture: embedded EWM (Scenario A) vs decentralised EWM (Scenario B).

1.5 EWM–ATTP Add-on Features

The add-on delivers two key capability areas that are covered in detail in Section 3 of this article:

  • SAP Standard Radio Frequency User Interface (RFUI) — Pre-configured RF screen sequences for serialization-relevant warehouse processes, providing operators with a single scanning interface that handles both physical execution and serialization compliance simultaneously. See Section 3.1 for a full explanation.
  • ATTP Warehouse Toolbox — The integration engine that composes and posts EPCIS serialization event messages from EWM to ATTP, covering the full spectrum of warehouse activities from inbound receiving to outbound shipping. See Section 3.2 for a full explanation.

Together these two capabilities are what make the add-on more than an interface — they make it an embedded compliance mechanism within warehouse operations.

1.6 EWM Add-on for ATTP — Installation

Before any integration configuration can begin, the EWM add-on for ATTP software must be correctly installed in the EWM system. This is an SAP Basis activity and must be completed before the functional and technical teams can configure the integration. The approach differs slightly depending on whether EWM is embedded in S/4HANA or deployed as a decentralised system on the SCM platform.

Required software component

The add-on is delivered as an ABAP add-on component named STTPEW.

The software component has release dependencies — the EWM release and the ATTP release must be at compatible levels. For exact software component versions and compatibility requirements, refer to SAP Notes 2304555 and 2380100.

Customizing settings in EWM for SAP ATTP

Once the software component is installed, certain customizing parameters related to SAP ATTP must be maintained in the EWM system. The entry point for this customizing differs by deployment model:

  • S/4HANA embedded EWM — Since EWM and ERP share the same system, the ATTP-related customizing parameters are maintained under the STTPEC component in the general customizing. The relevant transaction is /STTPEC/CUSTGEN.
  • Decentralised EWM on SCM — The ATTP-related customizing parameters are maintained under the transaction /STTPEW/CUSTGEN in the decentralised EWM system.

The customizing covers the key parameters that govern how EWM communicates with ATTP with determining crucial info i.e., the logical system to connect, the warehouse location determination to trigger event, the sender name to be used in EPCIS event, etc.  For the full list of parameters and their values, follow the SAP ATTP configuration guide on the SAP Help Portal.

 

The installation and customizing of the EWM add-on is a prerequisite for all integration activities described in Sections 2 and 3. No RFC destinations, Toolbox configurations, or business function activations related to ATTP will function correctly until STTPEW is installed and the relevant customizing parameters has been maintained.
 
 

2. Basic Integration Approach

SAP EWM can be embedded in S/4HANA or deployed as a standalone decentralised system. In both scenarios, connectivity must be established between EWM and ERP, and between EWM and ATTP.

2.1 S/4HANA Embedded EWM

Here the client has one S/4HANA system and uses the EWM module present in the same box. The warehouse and ERP share the same database. This is the simplest integration because they are already living in the same SAP box.

  1. Activate the business function in S/4HANA
    Because it's embedded, there is no separate software to install. However, the business function LOG_LE_INTEGRATION  still needs to be explicitly activated within S/4HANA to enable ERP integration with EWM.
  2. Set up the internal bridge
    Even though ERP and EWM share a database, SAP still uses a queuing system to pass delivery documents between the ERP side and the EWM side to maintain data integrity. A dummy logical system must be created and an RFC destination set up to route data to the EWM engine.
  3. Master data integration
    Because they share a database, no CIF or ALE/IDocs are needed. Materials are extended to EWM warehouse management views — GTINs are carried across by default as part of the material master extension. Customers and vendors created as Business Partners are immediately available to the warehouse, and their GLNs are included in the BP integration. Note: even in S/4HANA embedded EWM, plants and shipping points are not automatically available in EWM. They must be integrated using the program /SAPAPO/CREATE_LOCATION. Additionally, the GLN for each plant is maintained in ECC transaction EANGLN and is not automatically integrated to EWM — it must be maintained manually in EWM, ensuring it exactly matches the value in EANGLN.
  4. Delivery distribution
    Configure delivery split rules and EWM-specific parameters — distribution mode and communication method (QRFC) — for the ERP warehouse. This tells the system: when a delivery is created for this plant and storage location, hand it over to the EWM engine for processing.

2.2 ERP Integration with decentralised EWM

Here the client runs EWM as a completely separate system from ERP — each with its own installation, database, and transport landscape. Both master data and transactional documents must be explicitly distributed across the system boundary.

 

An important distinction: master data and transactional data use different integration mechanisms, covered separately in the steps below.
  1. Activate business functions
    On the ERP side, the business function LOG_LE_INTEGRATION must be activated to enable ERP integration with EWM.
  2. Establish system connectivity
    A logical system referring to the EWM system and an RFC destination must be created in ERP to route the data to decentralised EWM, and vice versa. Both systems must recognise each other as trusted logical systems in the ALE landscape.
  3. Master data distribution via IDocs / ALE
    Materials, customers and vendors are distributed from ERP to EWM as IDocs over the ALE channel. Plants and shipping points needs to be manually created in EWM system (with basic/minimal organizational attributes) and then run the program /SAPAPO/CREATE_LOCATION in EWM to convert those organizational units into APO/SCM Location records.
     
    In the older landscape of SAP ECC connected to decentralised EWM on the SCM/APO platform, master data was distributed via CIF. CIF is an SCM-era technology and does not apply to S/4HANA-based landscapes. In brownfield ECC+SCM landscapes, expect CIF.
  4. Delivery integration via QRFC
    Deliveries are integrated from ERP using QRFC (queued Remote Function Call). Delivery data is packaged as a BAPI, placed into an outbound queue, transmitted via RFC, and received into the inbound queue of the target system (EWM). When goods issue is confirmed in EWM, a confirmation BAPI travels back to ERP triggering the inventory posting.
  5. Delivery distribution configuration
    The ERP warehouse must be configured as EWM-relevant in ERP system with distribution mode and communication method set — the same principle as embedded, but here the handoff crosses a genuine system boundary.

2.3 SAP ATTP and SAP EWM Integration

Regardless of whether EWM is embedded or decentralised, ATTP always sits as a separate standalone system. The EWM add-on for ATTP orchestrates communication between them.

  1. Business function activation — Relevant business functions  must be activated within the EWM system before the connection can be established. 
  2. System connectivity and communication — Unlike traditional ERP-to-EWM integrations that rely on IDocs or queued RFCs, the real-time EWM-to-ATTP bridge is built primarily on modern OData services.

    In EWM as part of SAP Basis activity, a logical system referring to ATTP must be defined, and RFC destinations and HTTP destinations must be created. A logical system referring to EWM should be created in ATTP system as well. The HTTP destination is required to capture events being sent from the current EWM instance — it is used by the Warehouse Toolbox functions and also by the RF test UI. 

    There are two options for the Warehouse Toolbox to communicate with ATTP: OData services or RFC. OData is used by default. A particular business function must be activated to switch to RFC communication instead. For EPCIS event trigger from EWM, a GLN for the business location and read point is required — the GLN can be determined from the plant location or from the party entitled to dispose, controlled via the customizing parameter USE_BP_ENTITLED_GLN.
  3. Master data synchronization — Both systems must share the same GTINs, business partner references, and plant references, orchestrated by the central ERP distributing master data to both EWM and ATTP.
  4. RF user interface configuration — The RF UI in EWM must be configured for warehouse operators. Standard Business Configuration Sets provide ready-to-use screens on handheld scanners.
  5. Transactional execution flow — Once the architecture is live, warehouse operations automatically trigger ATTP events: packing → aggregation, goods issue → shipping notification, receiving → receipt confirmation. Each is covered in Section 4.
For architects: the integration has two distinct layers — EWM↔ERP (inventory and delivery documents) and EWM↔ATTP (serialization events). A failure in the EWM↔ERP layer holds up goods movements. A failure in the EWM↔ATTP layer holds up serialization — and in a regulated pharma environment, the latter is the one that triggers a compliance incident.
 
 

3. EWM–ATTP Add-on Features — Deep Dive

The add-on delivers two integrated capabilities that work in tandem: the Radio Frequency User Interface that guides operators through serialization-aware warehouse processes, and the ATTP Warehouse Toolbox that translates every confirmed warehouse action into a structured compliance EPCIS event in ATTP.

3.1 SAP Standard Radio Frequency User Interface (RFUI)

Walk into any pharmaceutical warehouse running SAP EWM and you will see operators carrying handheld scanner devices — moving between storage bins, scanning barcodes on cartons and pallets, and confirming warehouse tasks on a small screen. This is the Radio Frequency User Interface, or RFUI. It is the operational front end of the warehouse — the point where the physical world and the SAP system meet.

The RFUI in EWM is SAP standard functionality — a highly configurable framework where each warehouse process is represented as a guided sequence of screens on the handheld device. Each screen asks the operator to scan or confirm one thing at a time: a bin, a handling unit, a serial number. The screens are deliberately simple, designed for the warehouse floor — fast, unambiguous, and operable with a scanner.

As part of the EWM add-on for ATTP, SAP delivers pre-configured RF screen sequences covering the key serialization-relevant logistics processes — inbound receiving, put-away, outbound picking, packing, and shipping — with an outbound picking scenario provided as a reference demo implementation. These are starting points that implementation teams extend and customise to match the specific scanning requirements of each warehouse.

What the add-on changes for RFUI

Without the EWM add-on for ATTP, an operator completing a task on the handheld is performing a purely physical act — a quantity moved, a bin updated, a warehouse order confirmed. ATTP is entirely unaware.

With the add-on in place, the RF screen sequence is extended to include serialization-relevant scanning steps — scanning the SSCC of a case or the SGTIN of an individual item. Each scan is immediately validated against ATTP in real time. If the serial number is not in the expected state, the scanner rejects it on the spot.

When the operator confirms the step, the ATTP Warehouse Toolbox fires in the background and posts the corresponding serialization EPCIS event to ATTP — automatically, without any additional action from the operator.

 
From the operator's perspective, nothing changes beyond scanning a barcode they were already going to scan. From the compliance perspective, everything changes — every scan is now a validated, documented serialization event in ATTP, timestamped and ready for regulatory reporting.

3.2 ATTP Warehouse Toolbox

If the RFUI is the face of the EWM–ATTP integration — the screens the operator sees — then the ATTP Warehouse Toolbox is its engine. It is a collection of backend functions whose purpose is to take what happens in a warehouse process and translate it into a structured serialization event that ATTP understands. In technical terms, it composes and sends EPCIS (Electronic Product Code Information Services) event messages from EWM to ATTP.

 

EPCIS is the global standard language for supply chain visibility events. Every serialization event — a pick, a pack, a shipment, a receipt — is expressed as an EPCIS message with a defined structure: what happened (business step), to which objects (EPC list), where (read point and location), and in what state (disposition). The ATTP Warehouse Toolbox is what constructs these messages from EWM warehouse data and delivers them to ATTP.

The three-step sequence

For every warehouse activity involving a serialized material, the Toolbox follows a consistent three-step sequence:

1. Serialization check - Is material serialized? If no — ATTP not invoked
2. Validate & buffer per scan - Synchronous call to ATTP per SSCC / SGTIN scanned
3. Compose & send EPCIS - On process confirmation Async event posted to ATTP
 
Step 1 — Serialization check. The Toolbox checks whether the material being processed is serialized. If it is not, ATTP is not involved at all. Non-serialized materials pass through EWM without any ATTP overhead — critical in mixed warehouses handling both serialized finished goods and non-serialized raw materials.

Step 2 — Validate and buffer. After each individual scan — each SSCC or SGTIN the operator scans — the Toolbox performs a fast synchronous validation against ATTP. Is this serial number in the correct state for this activity? ATTP responds immediately. If valid, the scanned object is buffered in the context of the current warehouse activity. If the warehouse process is subsequently cancelled, the buffer is released and ATTP is not updated.

Step 3 — Compose and send. When the warehouse process is saved and confirmed, the Toolbox reads the buffer, composes the EPCIS event message, and sends it to ATTP asynchronously. ATTP receives the event, updates the serialization repository, and initiates any required regulatory reporting.

 
The combination of synchronous validation per scan and asynchronous event posting on confirmation is deliberate. Validation must be immediate — the operator needs to know on the spot if a scan is wrong. Event posting can be asynchronous because the warehouse process is already complete by that point — the compliance record follows the physical event by milliseconds, not hours.

From EWM data to EPCIS — the mapping

One of the most important things the Toolbox does is map EWM warehouse data fields to the corresponding EPCIS event fields. The warehouse system speaks in terms of deliveries, handling units, plants, and storage locations. ATTP speaks in terms of EPCs, business steps, read points, and dispositions. The Toolbox bridges these two vocabularies automatically.

EWM warehouse data EPCIS event field What it represents

 

Scanned SSCC / SGTINEPC listThe serialized objects involved in the event — the "what"
Delivery documentBusiness transactionThe business document that initiated the warehouse activity — the "why"
Plant / warehouse numberRead pointThe physical location where the event was observed — the "where"
Sold-from / sold-to locationSource / destination locationOrigin and destination of the serialized objects in the supply chain
Toolbox activity (e.g. Pick, Ship)Business step + dispositionWhat happened and what state the objects are in — derived automatically from the activity selected, no manual input required

The last row is worth highlighting. The business step and disposition — two of the most important EPCIS fields from a regulatory standpoint — are not entered by the operator. They are derived automatically from the Toolbox activity selected.

When the activity is Pick, the Toolbox knows the correct business step and disposition for a picking event. When the activity is Ship, it knows the correct values for a shipping event. This automatic derivation eliminates a significant source of human error in serialization reporting.

The breadth of Toolbox activities

The Toolbox covers the full spectrum of warehouse activities relevant to serialization — every major warehouse movement has a corresponding function:

Category Toolbox activities supported

 

Inbound processingGoods receipt by HU, Put-away, Receive document
Outbound processingPick (item/hierarchy), Pick by HU, Pick to pallet, Load, Ship
Internal processingPack (aggregate), Unpack (disaggregate), Commission, Decommission, Repack, Counting, Inspecting, Sampling
 
For architects and implementation teams: the Toolbox follows a clear paradigm — the warehouse process is always the leading process. ATTP is invoked only when necessary. This selective invocation is what makes the integration operationally viable in mixed pharmaceutical warehouses where serialized finished goods and non-serialized raw materials move through the same facility.
 
 

4. Processes Impacted

When EWM and ATTP exist as two separate, unconnected systems, every warehouse process that touches serialized goods creates a gap. The add-on closes these gaps by making serialization an embedded part of warehouse execution. The following sections walk through each impacted process — the end-to-end flow, what changes with the add-on, and the business value delivered.

 
4.1 Inbound Process
 
 
Fig 4.1 — Inbound process flow

The inbound process spans four systems and follows a clear sequence — from order creation, through physical receipt at the warehouse, to batch closure.

1. Process order and batch integrated to ATTP. The flow begins in S/4HANA with the creation of a process order and a batch. Both are immediately integrated into ATTP, so the serialization repository is aware of the expected production run before a single pallet reaches the warehouse.

2. Production, physical receipt, and goods receipt per pallet. At the lines, the MES/Line system drives serialization and packing — items are serialized, aggregated into cases, and assembled into pallet-level SSCCs. The physical pallets then move to the warehouse, where they are received one by one. Each pallet is scanned, EWM performs goods receipt, and put-away follows.

Each pallet-level goods receipt in EWM is replicated to the ERP inbound delivery. From there, ERP posts a receiving event to ATTP at batch level, updating the produced quantity with every pallet scan. In effect, this receiving event is how ATTP is told: for this batch, this quantity has now been received. Once all pallets for the delivery have been received, the goods receipt is completed at the ERP inbound delivery — GR Completion status is set to C — and ATTP reflects the full produced quantity correctly updated at batch level.

3. Commissioning, aggregation, and auto-receive at pallet level. Separately, the MES serialization and palletization step posts commissioning and aggregation events directly to ATTP, building the serial number hierarchy. Pallets are then auto-received in ATTP — a receiving event at the pallet level, distinct from the batch-level receiving event described above — and the serialized quantity is updated at batch level.

This brings in an important distinction: serialized quantity versus produced quantity. Serialized quantity comes from the packaging lines once items are commissioned and packed. Produced quantity reflects pallets physically received at the warehouse after being shipped from the lines. These two quantities must reconcile, and any mismatch needs to be investigated thoroughly, with the appropriate decommission, destroy, or lost event posted in ATTP to account for the difference.

4. Close of batch and process order closure. Once production and receipt are complete, the batch is closed at the lines. This signals S/4HANA to post goods receipt on the inventory and financial side and to close the process order, bringing the inbound cycle to completion.

 
4.2 Pack / repack — ad hoc packing
 
 
Fig 4.2 — Pack / repack process flow

The pack/repack process is a purely warehouse-internal operation with no S/4HANA involvement. It is initiated when goods need to be repacked at the warehouse — to consolidate, split, or repackage handling units.

An ad hoc HU warehouse task is created in EWM. The pallet is physically moved to the packing area, where repacking is performed. This is the ATTP-impacted step: once repacking is confirmed in EWM, an aggregation update is posted to ATTP reflecting the new handling unit hierarchy (Unpacking the old pallet, repacking the hierarchy to new Pallet). The pallet is then moved back to its original storage bin.

From a compliance perspective, any ad hoc repackaging at the warehouse is immediately reflected in the ATTP serialization repository — maintaining an accurate hierarchy at all times without any manual intervention.
 
4.3 Destruction — scrapping process
 
 
Fig 4.3 — Destruction process flow  

In pharmaceutical supply chains, serialized goods are typically shipped to a specialist facility for destruction — sensitive chemicals require certified processes and specialist equipment. The destruction flow in EWM is therefore structured as an outbound process to an external destruction facility.

The process is initiated in S/4HANA, which creates an outbound delivery. This delivery is distributed to EWM, where warehouse orders and warehouse tasks are created for picking the goods from their storage bins.

Picking is an ATTP-impacted step — in a partial pallet pick scenario, items are taken from the main pallet and packed into an intermediate picking handling unit (PICK-HU), triggering an aggregation update in ATTP. For a full pallet pick, no hierarchy update is required. An optional packing step may follow, also triggering an aggregation update.

When goods issue is posted in EWM, the post goods issue (PGI) is posted in S/4HANA updating inventory, and a decommission event is posted to ATTP with all pallet references, the delivery reference, and a reason code — for example, damaged, expired, or lost. The decommission event permanently removes the serial numbers from the active supply chain.

 
4.4 Outbound — picking, loading and goods issue
 
 
 Fig 4.4 — Outbound process flow

The outbound process is the most compliance-critical moment in the warehouse — it is when serialized goods leave the company's control and enter the downstream supply chain.

A sales order is created in S/4HANA, from which an outbound delivery is generated. The delivery is distributed to EWM and simultaneously integrated into ATTP — from this point ATTP is aware of the expected shipment and the delivery reference that will be attached to all subsequent serialization events.

EWM creates warehouse orders and warehouse tasks. If SSCCs are managed in ATTP, a request for SSCC is made to ATTP at this stage for the new handling unit required in partial picking scenarios.

Picking is an ATTP-impacted step — in the case of partial pallet picking, items are repacked into a new handling unit and the aggregation hierarchy is updated in ATTP. An optional packing step may also trigger an aggregation update. Loading of pallets onto the truck is an ATTP-impacted step — a picking/loading event is posted to ATTP and the delivery is assigned to the pallet, formally establishing the pallet-to-delivery relationship in ATTP.

Finally, goods issue is posted in EWM and replicated as a PGI in S/4HANA. A shipping event is posted to ATTP with all pallet references and the delivery reference, and the delivery status is marked as Closed in ATTP.

 

The loading event formally binds the physical pallets to the outbound delivery in ATTP. Without it, the shipping event at goods issue cannot be fully populated with the correct pallet-to-delivery relationship.

What the add-on delivers — across all processes

  • Business value - Compliance is built into the process, not bolted on after it. Regulatory obligations are met at the moment of the physical event — not deferred to a manual step that may be late, incorrect, or missed.
  • Operational value - Warehouse staff work in one system. Exceptions surface at the earliest possible point. Supervisors have a single, reliable view of execution and serialization status.
  • Technical value - Event-driven and synchronous — EWM and ATTP are always in step. Custom logic added through BADI hooks keeps the solution upgrade-safe and maintainable.
 

Closing Thoughts

The EWM add-on for ATTP looks deceptively simple on a slide and reveals its true complexity only when you are deep in an implementation. The technology works. But success depends far more on process design, master data governance, and exception handling than on configuration steps alone.

Design for exceptions first. The happy path is straightforward. ATTP is down, the ASN is wrong, the operator scanned the wrong barcode — these scenarios define whether your go-live is a success or a crisis.

Master data is not a project task — it is a program. EWM and ATTP alignment must be maintained continuously. Build a governance process from day one.

Involve your compliance team as architects. They know the regulatory requirements better than any systems integrator. Their input on what ATTP must report, and when, shapes every EWM process design decision.

 
Authors - 
Harshendu Dave
SAP EWM–ATTP Solution Architect
 
Gaurav Kochhar
SAP EWM–ATTP  Senior Solution Architect

entry.title: From Alerts to Autonomous Action: Building AI Agents for EWM Exception Handling with Joule
entry.content:
If you've spent any time in the Warehouse Monitor, you know the drill: a wave of alerts fires, a warehouse task fails, a bin comes up empty during putaway, and a key user goes hunting through node after node to figure out what broke and why. It works - but it's reactive, manual, and it doesn't scale as warehouses get busier and leaner on staff.

At the same time, SAP has been telegraphing a shift toward agentic AI across its logistics portfolio - Joule agents, "AI for Logistics," and sessions like Managing Warehouse Incidents with AI Agents at LogiMAT 2026. The vision is compelling: instead of a human triaging every exception, an agent monitors, reasons, and acts - closing the loop without a person in the middle for the routine cases.

What's missing from the conversation so far is the practical, EWM-specific version of this story: which exceptions are actually good candidates for agentic handling, what would the architecture look like, and where do you draw the guardrails? That's what this post digs into.

Start with the exceptions you already know

Before talking about agents, it helps to inventory what "exception handling" looks like in EWM today. A few familiar examples:

  • No empty bin found during automatic putaway (common after a Usage Decision/quality posting change or a bin-to-bin transfer).
  • Warehouse Task (WT) failures due to blocked resources, HU inconsistencies, or storage type capacity checks.
  • Wave/Resource imbalance - one activity area is drowning in open tasks while another sits idle.
  • RF confirmation errors - quantity mismatches, missing HUs, or expired batches surfacing mid-pick.

Today, each of these routes to a human: a key user checks the Warehouse Monitor, applies judgment, and manually triggers a fix (reassign a bin, cancel and recreate a WT, rebalance a resource group). It's exactly the kind of "detect → decide → act" loop that agentic AI is built for - provided the decision space is bounded and the action is reversible or low-risk.

What an agent actually adds

An AI agent isn't magic - it's a loop of three capabilities layered on top of what already exists in EWM:

  1. Perception - reading Warehouse Monitor alerts, exception codes, and queue/resource status in near-real time (via APIs rather than a human staring at a screen).
  2. Reasoning - using a model (Joule, or a custom LLM-backed service) to interpret the exception in context: is this a one-off, or the third "no empty bin" alert in this storage type this hour?
  3. Action - calling back into EWM (via released APIs / RFC-enabled function modules / OData services) to execute a bounded corrective action: reassign a destination bin, trigger a replenishment WT, or escalate to a human if confidence is low.

The key architectural point: the agent doesn't replace EWM's process logic - it sits alongside it as an orchestration layer, watching outputs and calling the same interfaces a key user or an RF device would use.

A worked example

Take the classic "no empty bin found after UD" scenario from quality inspection stock release:

  • Today: the WT fails, an alert appears in the Monitor, a key user investigates, checks storage type capacity, manually assigns an alternate bin, and re-releases the task.
  • With an agent: the event fires into the agent, which checks (a) is there genuinely no capacity, or a data/master-data issue, (b) are there eligible bins in an adjacent storage section that meet putaway strategy rules, and (c) has this happened repeatedly for this material/storage type combination (a signal for a slotting problem, not a one-off). Based on that, it either auto-assigns a valid alternate bin and re-triggers the WT, or escalates with a recommendation ("storage type 0020 is at 94% capacity - consider a slotting review") rather than just raising a raw error.

Notice what changed: the system logic for finding a valid bin hasn't moved - EWM still owns that. What the agent adds is the judgment call of when to act automatically vs. flag for a human, plus a bit of pattern recognition across repeated exceptions that a person triaging one alert at a time would likely miss.

Where the guardrails need to be

This is the part that tends to get glossed over in vendor demos, so it's worth being explicit:

  • Bound the action space. An agent should only be allowed to trigger actions from a pre-approved, low-risk set (bin reassignment within existing storage-type rules, resource rebalancing, WT recreation) - not master data changes or anything touching financial postings.
  • Confidence thresholds and human-in-the-loop fallback. If the agent isn't confident, the default should be escalate, not guess. This is a warehouse floor, not a chatbot - a wrong autonomous action has physical, inventory-accuracy consequences.
  • Full audit trail. Every agent-triggered action should be logged with the same rigor as a manual change (who/what triggered it, based on what reasoning), both for compliance and for tuning the agent over time.
  • Start narrow. Pick one or two exception types with clear, well-understood resolution logic (bin reassignment is a great first candidate) before expanding scope. Resist the urge to let an agent "handle exceptions" broadly on day one.

The takeaway

Agentic AI in EWM isn't about replacing the Warehouse Monitor or the key user - it's about narrowing the gap between "alert fired" and "problem fixed" for the well-understood, repetitive exceptions that currently eat up key-user time. The technology to start experimenting with this exists today in the SAP ecosystem (Joule, BTP, EWM's existing APIs); what's been missing is a clear-eyed, practitioner-level conversation about how to apply it responsibly. Hopefully this is a useful starting point for that conversation.

Have you experimented with agent-based automation around EWM exceptions - even informally, with scripts or bots? I'd love to hear what's worked (and what hasn't) in the comments.

entry.title: Manyat Thinking: Connecting MM, TM & Yard — Using Ad-hoc ASN HU Speed Layer
entry.content:
Manyat Thinking: Connecting MM, TM & Yard — Using Ad-hoc ASN HU Speed Layer to Eliminate Dock Bottlenecks in SAP ewm

Manyat Thinking | Business First, SAP Second

Introduction

When I look at warehouse execution, I do not like to start with configuration. I prefer to start with the physical operation and ask a simple business question: where is the warehouse actually losing time?

In inbound operations, the discussion often starts around the dock, staging, Goods Receipt, putaway, or warehouse task creation. But the physical journey starts earlier. The truck is already in the yard, the Transportation Unit may already be known, the inbound delivery may already exist, and expected material and Handling Unit information may already be available through the integrated MM, TM, and EWM process.

This made me look at the process differently.

If the warehouse already knows what is expected to arrive, why should the physical movement from the yard toward the dock door always depend on the completion of every downstream execution step?

The objective is not to bypass Goods Receipt. It is not to treat expected stock as confirmed inventory. It is not to remove warehouse control.

The objective is much simpler:

Can we use the information already available before GR to make the Yard-to-Door movement faster while keeping that movement controlled?

This is where my Manyat Thinking begins.

If the warehouse already knows what is coming, the physical operation should be ready to act on that information.

In this concept, I am looking at the Ad-Hoc HU Warehouse Task as a Speed Layer for Yard-to-Door movement, supported by an Internal Warehouse Process Type as the Control Layer.

Start With the Business Problem, Not the Configuration

Before discussing any SAP transaction, WPT, storage type, or RF menu, consider the physical situation.

A truck arrives in the yard.

The warehouse knows which inbound movement is expected. The transportation context is available. The inbound information is available in EWM. The Handling Units may already be identifiable through the expected inbound process.

The physical operation is ready.

But imagine that the truck still has to wait because the next system-driven execution step is not yet available.

From the system perspective, the process may still be progressing.

From the business perspective, however, one valuable resource is being consumed:

the truck and the dock capacity.

A dock door is not simply another warehouse location. It is a limited operational resource.

When a vehicle occupies a door longer than necessary, the impact can extend beyond that single truck. Another vehicle may have to wait. Yard congestion can increase. Operators can become unavailable for the next activity. Overall turnaround time can increase.

So instead of asking only:

“Has Goods Receipt happened?”

I would also ask:

“Does the physical Yard-to-Door movement really need to wait for the next downstream system step?”

That is the business problem I want to solve.

The Yard Is Already Part of Warehouse Execution

The yard is sometimes treated as a waiting area between transportation and warehouse execution.

Operationally, I see it differently.

The truck has arrived. Its transportation context is known. The inbound requirement is known. EWM may already have expected information about the delivery and Handling Units.

The important distinction is that this information represents expectation, not confirmed inventory.

That distinction should remain clear throughout the process.

Expected information can help the warehouse prepare and organize the physical movement.

Confirmed information is still required for inventory-related control.

Therefore, the concept is not about pretending that GR has already happened.

It is about using available information intelligently before GR.

The Core Idea: Ad-Hoc as the Speed Layer

This is the main idea behind the design.

For the Yard-to-Door movement, the warehouse may need flexibility because physical operations do not always happen exactly according to the original plan.

A truck can arrive earlier or later than expected. A particular door may become available. The physical yard position may change. Another operational condition may require the HU to be moved immediately.

In such situations, waiting for every predefined execution step can introduce unnecessary delay.

This is where an Ad-Hoc HU Warehouse Task can be used as an operational Speed Layer.

The purpose is not to replace standard EWM warehouse task management.

The purpose is to give the operator a controlled mechanism to execute the required physical movement when the operation needs speed.

The physical concept is:

Yard → Ad-Hoc HU Warehouse Task → Door

The Ad-Hoc task provides the execution flexibility.

But flexibility alone is not enough.

It must operate within warehouse rules.

That is where the Internal WPT comes in.

Ad-Hoc Provides Speed. Internal WPT Provides Control.

I consider these two elements complementary, not competing.

The Ad-Hoc HU Warehouse Task is the execution mechanism that allows the operator to react to the actual physical situation.

The Internal Warehouse Process Type provides the process control for that internal movement according to the warehouse design.

This creates a simple architectural separation:

Ad-Hoc HU WT = Speed

Internal WPT = Control

The operator is not simply performing an untracked physical movement.

The movement is represented through an EWM warehouse task and executed within the defined warehouse process.

That is why I describe this as a Speed Layer, not a shortcut.

The objective is to make execution faster without removing control.

Yard-to-Door Is the Key Movement

The most important clarification in this concept is where the Ad-Hoc movement is being used.

I am specifically applying the Ad-Hoc HU Warehouse Task to the:

Yard → Door

movement.

The door is the operational destination for the truck/HU movement in this speed layer.

The purpose is to bring the physical HU from the yard into the appropriate door location so that the receiving operation can proceed.

The concept can therefore be represented as:

MM / TM Expected Information
            ↓
     EWM Inbound Visibility
            ↓
           Yard
            ↓
 Ad-Hoc HU Warehouse Task
      + Internal WPT
            ↓
        Door Bin
            ↓
          Stage
            ↓
           GR
            ↓
        Putaway

The important point is that the Ad-Hoc Speed Layer ends at the Door.

It is not being introduced as a generic solution for every inbound movement.

It is solving one specific operational problem:

How can we move the HU from the yard toward the door without creating unnecessary physical waiting?

Why Represent the Door in EWM?

Physically, a dock door is a physical location where the truck is positioned and the unloading process takes place.

From an EWM perspective, the physical operation can be represented through an appropriate warehouse location/bin structure.

This gives the system a meaningful reference for where the HU is physically located during execution.

The design is therefore not simply:

“Create a bin because we need another bin.”

The business question comes first:

Do we need system visibility of the HU at the door?

If the answer is yes, then the door can be represented appropriately within the EWM warehouse structure based on the warehouse design.

The physical door and the EWM location then become connected representations of the same operational point.

This is another example of Business First, SAP Second.

MM and TM: Use the Information That Already Exists

The concept also depends on looking at the complete supply chain rather than treating EWM as an isolated system.

SAP MM provides the procurement expectation through the purchasing process.

SAP TM can provide transportation planning information and the Transportation Unit context.

SAP EWM receives and manages the relevant inbound warehouse information.

Therefore, before Goods Receipt, the warehouse may already have meaningful information about the expected inbound movement.

The point is not to create another planning layer.

The point is to use the information already available across the integrated process.

This leads to a simple Manyat principle:

Do not wait for new information when the existing process already provides enough information to prepare the physical operation.

Expected Data Is Not Confirmed Inventory

This distinction is critical.

Suppose an inbound shipment is expected to contain 20 Handling Units.

The warehouse can use that expected information to prepare the yard and door operation.

But if only 18 Handling Units physically arrive, the system must not treat the remaining two as received inventory simply because they were expected.

Expected information supports preparation.

Physical confirmation supports inventory control.

Goods Receipt remains an important control point for confirming the actual receipt according to the business process.

Therefore, this concept does not mean:

“Move stock before GR and treat it as received.”

It means:

“Use expected information to support physical movement before GR, while keeping inventory confirmation separate.”

That distinction protects the business process.

What Happens After the Door?

Once the HU reaches the appropriate door location, the Speed Layer has achieved its objective.

The truck can be positioned and the receiving operation can continue.

From there, the HU can move toward the staging area according to the warehouse's inbound process.

The staging area has a different operational purpose.

The Speed Layer is focused on the Yard-to-Door movement.

The subsequent receiving and inventory control activities can continue through the normal warehouse process, including the relevant verification, Goods Receipt, and downstream execution steps.

Therefore, I would not extend the Ad-Hoc concept unnecessarily into every subsequent inbound activity.

Keep the responsibility clear.

Yard-to-Door = Speed Layer

Stage and subsequent receiving activities = Control / Receiving Layer

This separation keeps the architecture simple.

Why Not Use Ad-Hoc Everywhere?

This is an important solution-design question.

If Ad-Hoc provides flexibility, why not use it for every movement?

Because flexibility should have a business reason.

If a movement is predictable, repetitive, and suitable for system-driven warehouse task creation, standard automation may be the better choice.

Ad-Hoc becomes valuable where the operation needs immediate flexibility and the physical situation cannot always be predicted perfectly.

Therefore, I would not design an entire warehouse around Ad-Hoc movements.

I would use it selectively where it solves a real operational problem.

This is an important part of Manyat Thinking:

Use automation where the process is predictable. Use flexibility where the operation genuinely needs flexibility.

The Standard SAP EWM Enablers

Only after defining the business requirement do I look at the SAP capabilities that can support it.

The concept can be implemented using standard SAP EWM capabilities, subject to the specific warehouse configuration and process design.

The Yard and Door locations can be represented through the appropriate EWM storage structure and permissions.

The relevant internal warehouse process can be controlled through an Internal WPT.

The operator can use the relevant RF process for creating and confirming the Ad-Hoc HU Warehouse Task.

The result is a controlled EWM warehouse movement rather than an informal physical relocation.

The technical objects are therefore supporting the business design.

They are not the starting point of the design.

That distinction is important.

Business requirement first.

SAP capability second.

Configuration last.

The Complete Manyat Architecture

When MM, TM, and EWM are viewed together, the concept becomes easier to understand.

The upstream process creates the expectation.

Transportation provides the movement context.

EWM provides warehouse visibility.

The yard becomes the physical starting point.

The Ad-Hoc HU Warehouse Task provides the operational speed required for the Yard-to-Door movement.

The Internal WPT keeps that movement within the defined warehouse control.

The door becomes a visible operational location in EWM.

The receiving process then continues toward staging, Goods Receipt, and putaway.

The complete concept is:

MM Expected Information
          ↓
TM Transportation Context
          ↓
EWM Inbound / TU Visibility
          ↓
        YARD
          ↓
Ad-Hoc HU WT + Internal WPT
          ↓
       DOOR BIN
          ↓
        STAGE
          ↓
          GR
          ↓
       PUTAWAY

Each layer has a clear responsibility.

MM: What is expected?

TM: How is the transportation movement planned?

EWM: How is the warehouse movement represented and controlled?

Ad-Hoc HU WT: How can the operator execute the required physical movement quickly?

Internal WPT: What movement rules apply?

Door: Where is the HU physically positioned for receiving?

Stage: Where does the receiving operation continue?

GR: What has actually been received?

Putaway: Where does the confirmed inventory continue?

This separation is what makes the design meaningful.

The Business Value

The value of this concept is not the Ad-Hoc transaction itself.

The value is the operational problem it can help address.

Dock doors are limited resources.

If a vehicle remains blocked at a door while the warehouse waits for an unnecessary downstream execution dependency, the warehouse loses capacity.

A controlled Yard-to-Door Speed Layer can help reduce that waiting and improve the physical flow.

Depending on the warehouse process and implementation, the potential benefits can include better dock utilization, reduced vehicle waiting time, lower yard congestion, improved operator utilization, and greater flexibility in inbound execution.

The exact result will always depend on the actual warehouse process, integration, configuration, and operational discipline.

But the design question remains valid:

If the physical operation is ready, why should the warehouse create unnecessary waiting?

The Question I Would Ask Before Changing SAP

This is perhaps the most important part of my thinking.

When I see a warehouse process that is slow, my first question is not:

“Which SAP transaction can fix this?”

My first question is:

“Where exactly is the physical operation waiting?”

Then I ask:

“Why is it waiting?”

And finally:

“Does that waiting provide real business control, or is it simply a system dependency?”

If the waiting is necessary for physical verification, compliance, quality, or inventory confirmation, then it has a business reason.

But if the physical movement can be safely controlled through a standard EWM mechanism while the warehouse is simply waiting for a downstream system step, then that part of the architecture deserves another look.

This is how I approach solution design.

Not:

Configuration → Process

But:

Business Problem → Physical Process → Business Requirement → SAP Capability → Configuration

That is the difference between configuring a system and designing a solution.

Manyat Thinking: Speed and Control Can Coexist

A warehouse should not have to choose between speed and control.

The right design can provide both.

The Ad-Hoc HU Warehouse Task can provide the operational flexibility required to move the HU from the yard toward the door when the physical operation needs immediate action.

The Internal WPT can provide the control required to keep that movement within the warehouse's defined process.

Goods Receipt can remain the confirmation point for the actual receipt and inventory-related control.

So the architecture becomes simple:

Ad-Hoc gives Speed.

Internal WPT gives Control.

GR gives Confirmation.

This is the core of the concept.

Final Thoughts

The warehouse does not suddenly become aware of an inbound shipment when Goods Receipt is posted.

The information journey has already started.

MM may already know what is expected.

TM may already know the transportation context.

EWM may already know the inbound and TU information.

The truck is physically present in the yard.

The operator is ready to execute.

The question is whether the warehouse design allows the physical operation to use that available information without creating unnecessary waiting.

My proposal is not to bypass standard warehouse controls.

It is not to replace system-driven warehouse execution.

It is not to treat expected data as confirmed inventory.

It is to introduce a controlled Speed Layer for a specific physical problem: Yard-to-Door movement.

In this design, the Ad-Hoc HU Warehouse Task provides the operational speed, while the Internal WPT provides the movement control. Once the HU reaches the door, the normal receiving process can continue toward staging, Goods Receipt, and putaway.

The technology is standard.

The thinking is the differentiator.

And this is why I always prefer to start with the business question.

A dock door is a limited operational resource. If the warehouse already knows what is coming, why is the truck still waiting?

That is the question behind this design.

That is the question behind Manyat Thinking.

Manyat Principle:

Use expected data to prepare. Use Ad-Hoc HU WT for operational speed. Use Internal WPT to keep that speed controlled. Use Goods Receipt for confirmed inventory control.

Business First. SAP Second.

— Rahul Kumar | Manyat Thinking

entry.title: The Missing Layer in Autonomous Warehousing: Warehouse Decision Memory
entry.content:
The Missing Layer in Autonomous Warehousing: Warehouse Decision Memory

 
Introduction
 
Warehouse Management systems are very good at recording what happened in the warehouse. But there is another layer of knowledge that is often missing — the reasoning behind the decisions experienced warehouse supervisors make every day. In this blog, I explore the concept of Warehouse Decision Memory and how SAP EWM, together with AI and SAP BTP, could capture these decisions, their context and outcomes to gradually build more intelligent warehouse execution.
 

I keep seeing the same thing in warehouse operations: the best supervisors often make decisions that the system did not recommend.

Your best supervisor makes a decision that isn't exactly what the system recommended. Maybe they change a task priority, move an operator to a different zone, or trigger replenishment earlier than planned. Most of the time, there's a good reason behind it.

I have seen this happen in real operations discussions: the system looks correct on paper, but the supervisor has a dock constraint, a delayed truck, or a customer escalation in mind that the standard strategy simply does not know at that moment.

The problem is that EWM records what happened, but not really why the decision was made. That knowledge stays with the person - and when they move to another site, change roles, or leave the organization, a lot of that experience leaves with them.

What if we could capture that knowledge?

This is where I feel AI in EWM can help in a practical way. I would call it Warehouse Decision Memory. The idea is simple:

System Recommendation → Warehouse Context → Human Decision → Outcome → Learning

For example, EWM recommends this sequence:

Putaway → Replenishment → Picking

But the supervisor changes it to:

Replenishment → Picking → Putaway

Why? It could be any of these:

  • A priority truck is leaving soon
  • Stock for an important order is running low
  • A specific operator happens to be available in that zone
  • There's congestion building up elsewhere
  • The goods carry a higher business priority
  • The supervisor just knows something the standard rules don't see

Today, that reasoning usually isn't captured anywhere in a structured way. That's the part worth fixing.

It is not only about adding one more KPI

Warehouses already run with many KPIs - distance, labor utilization, task age, throughput, resource availability. All of them matter. But in my experience, good supervisors do not decide based on one number alone. They look at what is happening on the floor and then take a call.

That is the part AI agents will eventually need to understand. Not just:

"Which task is closest?"

But:

"Given the current warehouse situation, which decision creates the highest operational value?"

And that answer can change from one minute to the next.

How I would start thinking about this

I do not think we need to rebuild EWM for this. EWM already has a lot of the operational picture. What is missing is the reason why a person moves away from the system recommendation, and what was happening in the warehouse at that time:

  • Open outbound demand
  • Delivery priority
  • Resource availability
  • Exception backlog
  • Inventory situation
  • Truck and dock constraints
  • Travel distance
  • Time of day

Then capture the outcome that followed: Did the order ship on time? Was an SLA breach avoided? Did the decision create rework, or reduce congestion?

Over time, patterns start to emerge.

This is the part I find interesting

Think of a situation where an AI agent looks at the current warehouse condition and says:

"The standard strategy recommends putaway first. However, in 78 similar situations, supervisors prioritized replenishment when outbound demand was within 60 minutes - and those decisions were associated with better on-time shipment performance."

To me, that is much more useful than a static rule saying "replenishment has higher priority." The agent is not just following a rule. It is learning from similar situations, the context around them, and the outcome that followed - while the supervisor still has the final say.

One thing we should be careful about

We can't assume every good outcome was caused by the decision that preceded it. Warehouse operations are complex - a truck leaving on time may have nothing to do with one particular override.

So for me, the hard part is not only collecting more data. It is understanding whether that decision actually changed the outcome. Otherwise, we may just end up training a model on past transactions and confusing correlation with real learning.

Where I would begin

I would not try to capture every decision in the warehouse from day one. I would pick one clear use case - for example, manual task-priority overrides during peak operations - and capture:

Recommendation → Context → Decision → Outcome

Run it for one peak season and see what the data tells you.

If we can identify real patterns in how experienced supervisors make these calls, that would be valuable. We would not just be automating warehouse processes. We would be starting to retain some of the warehouse experience that usually stays in people's heads. For me, that is one of the missing pieces on the road to autonomous warehouse execution. The future warehouse should not only know what happened. It should slowly learn why experienced people chose to do something differently.

That is why I feel Warehouse Decision Memory is worth exploring.

Conclusion

The journey towards autonomous warehouse execution is not only about giving AI access to more data or automating more tasks. It is also about capturing the experience and decision-making that already exists on the warehouse floor. Warehouse Decision Memory could provide a way to turn those human decisions into reusable knowledge, helping future AI agents make more context-aware and explainable decisions while keeping humans in the loop.

Would love to hear from the EWM and warehouse community: are you already capturing the reasoning behind manual overrides, or only the final transaction? That might be the first real step toward a warehouse that learns.

entry.title: SAP Joule in SAP S4HANA Cloud Private Edition Navigation, Transactions & Fiori Launchpad
entry.content:
SAP Joule in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition: Navigation, Transactions & Fiori Launchpad Plug-In Configuration

Introduction

SAP Joule is SAP's generative AI copilot, deeply embedded within the SAP ecosystem to transform how users interact with enterprise applications. Rather than navigating complex menus or memorizing transaction codes, users can express their intent in natural language and let Joule guide them — whether that means navigating to the right SAP Fiori app, executing a transaction, retrieving information, or generating analytical insights. 

Joule is available for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition (2021 onwards), SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, SAP SuccessFactors, and SAP Build Code, and is unlocked through product licensing that includes Joule messages. 

Three SAP Notes are particularly important for anyone implementing or operating Joule in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition: 3751657, 3523238, and 3799821. Together, they address the activation, capabilities, and consulting boundaries of Joule — forming a practical reference triad for administrators, consultants, and power users alike.

SAP Note 3751657 – How to Configure and Activate Joule Plug-In in a Target Mapping (SAP Fiori Launchpad)

What it addresses: One of the most common early hurdles when deploying Joule in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition is making the Joule icon visible and accessible within the SAP Fiori Launchpad. SAP Note 3751657 directly addresses this challenge. 

Core guidance: To enable the Joule icon in the Fiori Launchpad of an S/4HANA Private Cloud system, the Joule Plug-In must be configured in a target mapping within the SAP Fiori Launchpad. The note provides step-by-step guidance (via an attached document) covering: 

  • Creating a Technical Catalog in the Launchpad App Manager using transaction /n/UI2/FLP
  • Configuring a target mapping with the intent Shell-plugin
  • Creating a new Role in Role Maintenance (/npfcg) and assigning the catalog to it
  • Assigning the JOULE_ADMIN technical user created during prerequisites 

Joule-specific impact: Without this configuration, the Joule icon simply does not appear in the Fiori Launchpad — meaning users have no entry point to the AI copilot, regardless of whether all other BTP-side configurations are correctly in place. This note is therefore a critical activation step in the end-to-end Joule setup journey. 

 

SAP Note 3523238 – Navigational and Transactional Capabilities with Joule in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition

What it addresses: Once Joule is activated, the natural next question is: what can it do? SAP Note 3523238 is the definitive reference for understanding the full scope of Joule's capabilities in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition. 

Core guidance: The note outlines two primary capability types:

  • Navigational Capabilities: Joule navigates users to the relevant SAP Fiori app based on a natural language prompt. This is especially valuable for new or occasional users unfamiliar with individual app names. Supported areas include Procurement, Finance, Sales, Service Management, Production Planning, Extended Warehouse Management, and Resource Scheduling. Example prompts include "Which app should I use to clear a GL account?" or "Where can I manage warehouse tasks?" 
  • Transactional Capabilities: Users can carry out tasks directly within Joule — without opening the relevant SAP Fiori app. Supported areas include Finance, Sales, Procurement, Manufacturing, Asset Management, R&D Engineering, and Cross-area functions. Activation of the relevant OData services is a mandatory prerequisite for each transactional use case. 

The note also references two key attachments:

  • Joule for SAP S4HANA Cloud Private Edition Navigational Capabilities.xlsx — a detailed list of all Fiori apps enabled for Joule navigation
  • Business Roles and API for Transactional Capabilities.xlsx — the associated business roles and OData services required per transactional use case 

For issues related to Joule capabilities, the note directs users to raise tickets under component CA-FLP-EXT-PCE-JOULE, and references SAP Note 3746234 (Role and OData Analyser) for verifying custom roles and OData activation status. 

Joule-specific impact: This note is the single most important reference for Joule capability planning. It enables administrators and consultants to map business requirements to specific Joule features, identify the exact OData services to activate, and assign the correct business roles to users — all of which are prerequisites for Joule to deliver transactional and navigational responses rather than falling back to generic informational replies. 

SAP Note 3799821 – Consulting Topics for Joule

Note: SAP Note 3799821 was not directly available in the verified sources reviewed. The closest matching SAP Note covering consulting scope, boundaries, and support classification for Joule is SAP Note 3704471 – Consulting Topics for Joule . The content below is based on that note. If SAP Note 3799821 covers a different specific topic, please verify its content directly on SAP for Me (me.sap.com).

What it addresses: Not every Joule issue is a support issue — and understanding this distinction saves significant time during implementation. SAP Note 3704471 (aligned with the consulting topics theme) clarifies which Joule-related issues fall under SAP Technical Support versus Consulting. 

Core guidance: The note establishes that many Joule issues stem from faulty or insufficient integration with other SAP products, rather than product defects. Key classifications include: 

  • Out of scope for Technical Support: Joule end-to-end initial configuration, licensing and entitlement questions, "how-to" questions, and customer-specific setup scenarios (e.g., configuring Joule without a shared Cloud Identity Service tenant or Global User ID)
  • In scope for Technical Support: Processing errors, "Digital Assistant not Found" messages, Internal Server Errors, and issues preventing Joule from functioning at all
  • Configuration-related issues (e.g., Joule returning generic informational responses instead of navigational/transactional results) are classified as Consulting, as they typically indicate an integration misconfiguration 

Consulting options available:

  • Cloud Readiness Service — validates that all prerequisites and configurations for Joule are correctly in place
  • AI Factory — provides guidance on setting up Joule
  • Expertise on Demand / SAP Consulting — for deeper engagement via your SAP Account Manager 

Joule-specific impact: This note helps teams set realistic expectations before raising support tickets and directs them to the right channel — whether self-service resources, consulting engagements, or technical support — based on the nature of their issue. 

Key Takeaways for SAP Joule Users

  • Activation is a multi-step process: Enabling Joule in the Fiori Launchpad requires explicit plug-in configuration in a target mapping (SAP Note 3751657). Do not assume Joule will appear automatically after BTP-side setup. 
  • Capabilities are role- and OData-dependent: Joule's transactional and navigational features only work when the correct business roles are assigned to users and the required OData services are activated in the back end. SAP Note 3523238 is your go-to reference for this mapping. 
  • Know the support boundary: Configuration issues are Consulting, not Support. If Joule is returning generic informational responses instead of executing navigational or transactional tasks, the root cause is almost always an integration or configuration gap — not a product defect. Use the Cloud Readiness Service or AI Factory for these scenarios. 
  • Joule respects your authorization model: Through Principal Propagation, Joule operates strictly within existing SAP S/4HANA authorization boundaries. Users can only access data and perform actions for which they already hold authorization. 
  • Release version matters: Not all Joule capabilities are available from release 2021. Higher releases unlock additional functionality. Always verify capability availability against your specific S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition release. 

Conclusion

SAP Joule represents a fundamental shift in how users interact with SAP S/4HANA — moving from menu-driven navigation to natural language conversation. However, realizing this potential requires careful attention to activation, capability configuration, and support boundaries.

SAP Notes 3751657, 3523238, and the consulting guidance note together form a practical implementation framework: activate Joule correctly in the Fiori Launchpad, configure the right roles and OData services for your desired capabilities, and understand where to turn when issues arise. With these foundations in place, organizations can unlock Joule's full potential — from navigating users to the right app in seconds, to executing transactions through conversation, to delivering analytical insights on demand.    

For the latest capability updates, always refer to the What's New for Joule documentation on SAP Help Portal, which is continuously updated with new use cases across S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, Public Edition and beyond. 

Refer to:

What's New for Joule | SAP Help Portal

3523238 - Navigational and Transactional capabilities with Joule in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition - SAP for Me (Consider Attachments).

3751657 - How to configure and activate Joule Plug-In in a target mapping (SAP Fiori Launchpad) - SAP for Me (Consider Attachments).

Hope this helps you!

Thank you and regards.

Rogerio Lima.

entry.title: SAP EWM Returnable Packaging Material GR 501 M Using BADI
entry.content:
Introduction

In many manufacturing and consumer goods industries, suppliers deliver materials using reusable packaging such as plastic totes, pallets, crates, containers, and reusable bins. While the purchased raw materials become company inventory through the normal procurement process, the packaging itself often remains vendor-owned and must be tracked separately.

During a recent SAP S/4HANA and SAP EWM implementation, we encountered a requirement to automatically create inventory postings for returnable packaging materials during Goods Receipt without requiring additional manual transactions by warehouse users.

This blog explains how we designed a solution using a BADI enhancement that automatically creates a returnable packaging item and posts it through Movement Type 501M during the inbound process. The approach eliminates manual posting activities and improves inventory accuracy. The overall business scenario is consistent with SAP returnable packaging processing and automatic generation of packaging-related delivery items documented in SAP resources.

Technical Design
